latin: Hanc me regulam professum, qua inseparatos ab alterutro patrem et filium et spiritum testor, tene ubique, et ita quid quomodo dicatur agnosces.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 41 = printed p. 11
english: Bear always in mind that this is the rule of faith which I profess; by it I testify that the Father, and the Son, and the Spirit are inseparable from each other, and so will you know in what sense this is said.
page: page unknown (New Advent HTML has no printed page numbers); Latin Latin printed p. 11
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: Tertullian states the rule of faith: Father, Son and Spirit are inseparable.
limits: Introduces the chapter; does not argue the Trinity itself. ANF is a 19th-century translation.

latin: ecce enim dico alium esse patrem et alium filium et alium spiritum, — male accipit idiotes quisque aut peruersus hoc dictum, quasi diuersitatem sonet et ex diuersitate separationem protendat patris et filii et spiritus sancti;
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 41 = printed p. 11
english: Understand then; I say that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Spirit another—every untrained or perverse person takes this saying wrongly, as if it expressed difference, and as the result of difference meant a separation of Father, Son and Holy Spirit;
page: 46 (inferred from running-head sequence; printed number absent from OCR; PDF p. 44)
edition: A. Souter, Tertullian Against Praxeas, Translations of Christian Literature Series II, Latin Texts (London: SPCK; New York: Macmillan, 1920); Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: Tertullian says each of Father, Son and Spirit is 'alium' (another), and that this word must not be heard as separation.
limits: The hard word is 'alium' (another). ANF (Holmes) renders it 'the Father is one, and the Son one, and the Spirit one', which hides the contrast; quote Souter or the Latin. Anti-Trinitarians read 'alium' as diversity of being; Tertullian denies this in the same sentence.

latin: non tamen diuersitate alium filium a patre, sed distributione, nec diuisione alium, sed distinctione, quia non sint idem pater et filius, uel modulo alius ab alio
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 41 = printed p. 11
english: it is not by way of diversity that the Son differs from the Father, but by distribution: it is not by division that He is different, but by distinction; because the Father is not the same as the Son, since they differ one from the other in the mode of their being.
page: page unknown (New Advent HTML has no printed page numbers); Latin Latin printed p. 11
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: The Son is 'other' than the Father by distribution and distinction, not by diversity or division.
limits: Tertullian does not define 'distributio' here. The pair 'distributio / divisio' is his own vocabulary; anti-Trinitarians answer that distinction of persons is still a difference of being.

latin: pater enim tota substantia est, filius uero deriuatio totius et portio, sicut ipse profitetur: quia pater maior me est.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 41 = printed p. 11
english: For the Father is the entire substance, but the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole, as He Himself acknowledges: My Father is greater than I. John 14:28
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3). Souter (1920) p. 46 reads: 'For the Father is all being, but the Son is a tributary of the whole and a portion'
edition: page unknown (New Advent HTML has no printed page numbers); Latin Latin printed p. 11; Souter 46 (inferred)
what_it_says: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
use: The Father is the whole substance; the Son is a derivation and portion of that whole; the Father is greater.
page_file_pdf_page: Opponents (subordinationists) cite 'tota substantia ... portio' and 'maior me est' against the Son's equality. Qualifiers in the same chapter: 'distinctione, non divisione'; 'alium' = distinction of persons. Ch. 12 (Latin printed p. 17) states 'unam substantiam in tribus cohaerentibus'. Tertullian's 'substantia' is not defined here; ch. 2 (T3-15) gives the triad of substance/status/power. I did not read other chapters to cross-check 'derivatio' (ANF 'derivation').

latin: a quo et minoratus canitur in psalmo modicum quid citra angelos. sie et pater alius a filio, dum filio maior, dum alius qui generat, alius qui generatur, dum alius qui mittit, alius qui mittitur, dum alius qui facit, alius per quem fit.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 41 = printed p. 11
english: In the Psalm His inferiority is described as being a little lower than the angels. Thus the Father is distinct from the Son, being greater than the Son, inasmuch as He who begets is one, and He who is begotten is another; He, too, who sends is one, and He who is sent is another; and He, again, who makes is one, and He through whom the thing is made is another.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3). Souter (1920) p. 46-47 reads 'another' for each 'alius' ('since it is one that begets, another that is begotten')
edition: page unknown (New Advent HTML has no printed page numbers); Latin Latin printed p. 11
what_it_says: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
use: 'Minoratus' (diminished, a little lower than the angels) is cited from Ps 8:6; the Father and Son are distinct as begetter/begotten, sender/sent, maker/made.
page_file_pdf_page: The 'minoratus' clause is the best-known hard point (Heb 2:7 quoting Ps 8:6). Tertullian's qualifier is the 'human' sufferings (ch. 14, outside my range: 'propter hoc minoratus a patre', Latin printed p. 25, read from OCR only, not checked on scan). The 'alius' pairs are relational, so they do not by themselves settle equality of substance.

latin: bene, quod et dominus usus hoc uerbo in persona paracleti non diuisionem significauit, sed dispositionem: rogabo enim, inquit, patrem, et 'alium' aduocatum mittet uobis, spiritum ueritatis, sic alium a se *paracletum, quomodo et nos a patre alium filium, ut tertium gradum ostenderet in paracleto, sicut nos secundum in filio propter oikonomiae obseruationem.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 41 = printed p. 11; the asterisk before 'paracletum' is printed
english: Happily the Lord Himself employs this expression of the person of the Paraclete, so as to signify not a division or severance, but a disposition (of mutual relations in the Godhead); for He says, I will pray the Father, and He shall send you another Comforter...even the Spirit of truth, John 14:16 thus making the Paraclete distinct from Himself, even as we say that the Son is also distinct from the Father; so that He showed a third degree in the Paraclete, as we believe the second degree is in the Son, by reason of the order observed in the Economy.
page: page unknown (New Advent HTML has no printed page numbers); Latin Latin printed p. 11
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: John 14:16 uses 'another' (alius) of the Paraclete; Tertullian says the Son is 'second' and the Spirit 'third' in the economy.
limits: The 'gradus' (degree) and 'second/third' vocabulary is economic in Tertullian's frame; opponents read 'secundum' as rank. ANF's 'disposition' is Latin 'dispositionem'. The asterisk and 'alium' in quotation marks are printed by Kroymann.

ref: 9 (chapter; locator 'ipsum, quod pater et filius dicuntur')
latin: ipsum, quod pater et filius dicuntur, nonne aliud ab alio <aliud> est? utique enim omnia quod uocantur, hoc erunt, et quod erunt, hoc uocabuntur, et permiscere se diuersitas uocabulorum non potest omnino, quia nec rerum, quarum erunt uocabula.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 42 = printed p. 12. Angle brackets <aliud> are Kroymann's supplement (conjecture), not a manuscript reading
english: Besides, does not the very fact that they have the distinct names of Father and Son amount to a declaration that they are distinct in personality? For, of course, all things will be what their names represent them to be; and what they are and ever will be, that will they be called; and the distinction indicated by the names does not at all admit of any confusion, because there is none in the things which they designate.
page: page unknown (New Advent HTML has no printed page numbers); Latin Latin printed p. 12
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: The names Father and Son are distinct, so the persons are distinct; the names cannot be confused.
limits: This is the 'alius non aliud' passage: the 'aliud' in the Latin is Kroymann's insertion in angle brackets. The argument is from names; it does not say what the one substance is.

ref: 9 - 10 (chapter 10 opening; locator 'Ita ut pater, et filius est')
latin: Ita ut pater, et filius est, et <ut> neque dies eadem et nox, neque pater idem et filius, ut sint ambo unus et utrumque alter, quod uanissimi isti Monarchiani uolunt.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 42 = printed p. 12. The <ut> is Kroymann's supplement
english: So both the Father 'is' and the Son 'is' (just as day is and night is); and neither is day the same as night, nor Father the same as Son. If they were, both would be one and either of the two would be both, as these foolish Monarchians make out.
edition: A. Souter, Tertullian Against Praxeas, Translations of Christian Literature Series II, Latin Texts (London: SPCK; New York: Macmillan, 1920); Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: Day and night are both 'is' but not the same; so Father and Son are both 'is' but not the same.
limits: Souter's footnote: C. H. Turner reads 'ita et pater et filius est' (different arrangement and reading). Kroymann prints 'ita ut' with <ut> supplied. The ANF text here reads 'So it is either the Father or the Son ...' and should not be quoted for this sentence.

latin: habeat necesse est pater filium, ut pater sit, et filius patrem, ut filius sit. aliud est autem habere, aliud esse, uerbi gratia, ut maritus sim, habeam oportet uxorem, non ipse mihi ero uxor.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 42 = printed p. 12
english: A father must needs have a son, to be a father, and a son must have a father, to be a son. It is one thing to have, another to be. For example, to be a husband I must have a wife; I shall not be myself a wife to myself.
edition: A. Souter, Tertullian Against Praxeas, Translations of Christian Literature Series II, Latin Texts (London: SPCK; New York: Macmillan, 1920); Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: Father and Son are correlatives: to be a father one must have a son; no one is his own son.
limits: A relational argument: it shows the Father and Son are not the same subject, and answers 'he made himself a son'. It does not, by itself, settle the question of substance. Ch. 10-11 (Souter pp. 48-52) continue the argument.

ref: 10 (chapter; locator 'potuit et Praxean ... oportebat et patrem crucifigi')
latin: potuit et Praxean et omnes pariter haereticos statim extinxisse; non tamen, quia potuit, extinxit. [oportebat enim et miluos esse et haereticos, oportebat et patrem crucifigi.] hac ratione erit aliquid et difficile deo, id scilicet, quodcumque non fecerit, non quia non potuerit, sed quia noluerit.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 43 = printed p. 13. The square brackets are Kroymann's and mark the sentence as suspect
english: He could have at once put to death both Praxeas and all other heretics alike; yet simply because He had the power He did not do so. For it was meet that there should be both kites and 'heretics,' it was also meet that the Father should be crucified! In this way there will be something even 'difficult to' God, namely, whatsoever He has not done, not because He could not, but because He willed not.
edition: A. Souter, Tertullian Against Praxeas, Translations of Christian Literature Series II, Latin Texts (London: SPCK; New York: Macmillan, 1920); Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: Tertullian argues God could have done many things and did not; the sentence 'it was meet that the Father should be crucified' is the one opponents cite.
limits: The bracketed sentence is the Patripassian crux: Kroymann's square brackets (in his apparatus convention, usually suspected interpolation) enclose it; Souter prints it without brackets. Do not present it as firm text without the bracket note. The defence is the 'possibility vs will' argument in the same sentence ('dei enim posse uelle est').

latin: unum tamen ueritus est: mentiri, — ueritus autem semetipsum et suam ueritatem — et ideo ueracem deum credens scio illum non aliter quam disposuit pronuntiasse nec aliter disposuisse quam pronuntiauit.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 44 = printed p. 14
english: Nay: one thing, however, He did fear; falsehood—being afraid of Himself and His own truth; and therefore believing God truthful I know that He has not declared differently from what He arranged, and has not arranged differently from what He declared.
edition: A. Souter, Tertullian Against Praxeas, Translations of Christian Literature Series II, Latin Texts (London: SPCK; New York: Macmillan, 1920); Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: God fears only falsehood, so His word and His arrangement agree; Tertullian argues God cannot be made self-contradictory.
limits: Souter's note 1 reports C. H. Turner's reading 'ueritatis auctorem' in place of the words translated 'ueritui/ueritus autem'. The scan prints 'ueritus autem'. This is a close argument from divine truthfulness, not an explanation of the Son's status.

latin: tu porro eum mendacem efficias et fallacem et deceptorem fidei huius, si, cum ipse esset sibi filius, alii dabat filii personam, quando scripturae omnes et demonstrationem et distinctionem trinitatis ostendant
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 44 = printed p. 14
english: But you would make Him untruthful and false, and a deceiver of these believers, if, although Himself a son to Himself, he gave to another the person of His Son, since all the Scriptures make the Trinity clear and the distinction within it,
edition: A. Souter, Tertullian Against Praxeas, Translations of Christian Literature Series II, Latin Texts (London: SPCK; New York: Macmillan, 1920); Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: Tertullian argues the Praxean reading makes God a deceiver, since Scripture shows the Trinity and distinction.
limits: The clause 'alii dabat filii personam' (gave to another the person of the Son) shows his use of 'persona' for distinct persons. Souter translates 'the distinction within it' (Latin 'distinctionem trinitatis'); this is a reductio against the opponent, not a positive account of unity of substance.

latin: 'dominus dixit ad se: filius meus sum ego, ego hodie generaui me'; proinde et: 'ante luciferum generaui me'; et: 'dominus condidi me initium uiarum in opera mea, ante omnes autem colles generaui me'
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 44 = printed p. 14
english: The Lord said to Himself: I am my son, I have this day begotten myself; in like manner also: 'Before the morning star I begat myself'; and: 'I the Lord created myself as a beginning of ways for my works, yea, before any of the hills were, I begat myself'
edition: A. Souter, Tertullian Against Praxeas, Translations of Christian Literature Series II, Latin Texts (London: SPCK; New York: Macmillan, 1920); Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: Tertullian reworks Ps 2:7, Ps 109:3 and Prov 8:22 with the Father as subject and the Son as object, to show the absurdity of the Praxean reading.
limits: This is a reductio, not a direct statement of doctrine. The Prov 8:22 'created' and Ps 109:3 'begat' are the texts anti-Trinitarians use for the Son's creation. Kroymann prints the Scripture quotations with single quote marks; these are reproduced as printed.

latin: alium autem quomodo accipere debeas, iam professus sum, personae, non substantiae nomine, ad distinctionem, non ad diuisionem. ceterum, <etsi> ubique teneo unam substantiam in tribus cohaerentibus, tamen alium dicam oportet ex necessitate sensus eum, qui iubet, et eum, qui facit.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 47 = printed p. 17 (read by eye: 'personae', OCR had 'gersonae')
english: In what sense, however, you ought to understand Him to be another, I have already explained, on the ground of Personality, not of Substance — in the way of distinction, not of division. But although I must everywhere hold one only substance in three coherent and inseparable (Persons), yet I am bound to acknowledge, from the necessity of the case, that He who issues a command is different from Him who executes it.
page: page unknown (New Advent HTML has no printed page numbers); Latin Latin printed p. 17
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: 'Other' means distinct in person (persona), not in substance; one substance in three coherent persons.
limits: The best key sentence for the brief. Note: '(Persons)' is ANF's addition in brackets; the Latin says only 'in tribus cohaerentibus'. The Latin reads 'personae' (ANF: 'Personality'); the OCR had misread it as 'gersonae'.

latin: tres autem non statu, sed gradu, nec substantia, sed forma, nec potestate, sed specie, — unius autem substantiae et unius status et unius potestatis, quia unus deus, ex quo et gradus isti et formae et species in nomine patris et filii et spiritus sancti deputantur.
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 33 = printed p. 3
english: three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance, and of one condition, and of one power, inasmuch as He is one God, from whom these degrees and forms and aspects are reckoned, under the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
page: page unknown (New Advent HTML has no printed page numbers); Latin Latin printed p. 3
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: The three are distinguished by degree, form and aspect, not by status, substance or power, and they share one substance, status and power.
limits: Outside the assigned range (ch. 9-12), included because the brief names this triad. Anti-Trinitarians read 'gradu' as rank. The sentence itself says 'unius autem substantiae', so it is a direct statement of unity of substance. Souter's note on the reading 'statu' was not checked.

latin: at ubi uenit Christus et cognitus est a nobis, quod ipse, qui numerum retro fecerat, factus secundus a patre et cum spiritu tertius, etiam pater, per ipsum plenius manifestatus, redactum est iam nomen dei et domini in unionem
latin_edition: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog; read from scan image (checked by eye) and archive.org OCR text; quotation marks and <brackets> as printed; scan PDF p. 49 = printed p. 19
english: As soon, however, as Christ came, and was recognised by us as the very Being who had from the beginning caused plurality (in the Divine Economy), being the second from the Father, and with the Spirit the third, and Himself declaring and manifesting the Father more fully (than He had ever been before), the title of Him who is God and Lord was at once restored to the Unity (of the Divine Nature)
page: page unknown (New Advent HTML has no printed page numbers); Latin Latin printed p. 19
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent HTML; Latin: E. Kroymann ed., Tertulliani Adversus Praxean (Tuebingen: J.C.B. Mohr, 1907), archive.org item tertullianadver00tertgoog
what_it_says: Christ, having made the plurality in the economy, became 'second from the Father' and 'third' with the Spirit, and manifested the Father more fully.
limits: Outside the assigned range (ch. 13), included for the brief's 'secundus' item. Opponents read 'factus secundus' as a becoming/creation. Tertullian's qualifiers: 'in the Divine Economy' and 'manifested more fully'. Only this sentence was checked on the scan; the rest of ch. 13 was read from OCR.
